notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Luke 2:27–52, drawn from the pages I was able to access:

---

## Luke 2:27–52 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

**v. 27: "Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts…"**

- **Ellicott** says "by the Spirit" is better rendered "in the Spirit" — indicating a spiritual state in which the power of the Divine Spirit was the pervading element (as in Revelation 1:10). Simeon was not merely directed by a sudden impulse but walked in a habitual spiritual condition. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2.htm)
- **Gill** notes that the Spirit, knowing the exact time Jesus would be brought to the temple, "suggested to Simeon, and moved upon him, and influenced and directed him, to go thither at that very time." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-27.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-27.htm)
- **Barnes** concisely states: "By the Spirit — By the direction of the Spirit," and adds Simeon went into the court of the women where public worship occurred. [biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/luke/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-27.htm)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** emphasizes Simeon "was a man who knew how to be led by the Holy Spirit, both in hearing God's promise to him and being prompted to go to the temple at the right time." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- On "the parents": **Ellicott** notes Luke does not shrink from reproducing the familiar phraseology of the Nazareth household, where Joseph was called Jesus' parent in common life. The older manuscripts read "his father" in v.33 for "and Joseph." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2.htm)
- **Ellicott** also notes that in common practice the child would have been presented to the priest; Simeon, though not a priest, takes on himself to receive the child. This fits with the idea of his being an Essene revered for prophetic gifts. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-27.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-27.htm)

---

**v. 28: "Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God…"**

- **Gill** writes: "That same Spirit that had revealed unto him that he should not die till he saw the Messiah … made known unto him that that child … was the Messiah; wherefore, in a rapture of joy, he took him out of their arms into his own." Some think Simeon was a priest presenting the firstborn; Gill finds the former account "more agreeable." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-28.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-28.htm)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** "Simeon's prophecy was filled with love for his Savior; and he hardly knew Jesus. We who know so much more about Him should love Him even more." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)

---

**vv. 29–32: The *Nunc Dimittis* — "Sovereign Lord, as You have promised…"**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Simeon now had the peace of seeing God's promise fulfilled. "It was as if Simeon were commanded by God to keep a lonely watch through the night until he saw the sun come up. This now was, for him, God's sunrise." The prophecy is remarkable because it shows salvation "was always to be extended beyond Israel" — a light for the Gentiles. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **Orthodox (OCA):** The *Nunc Dimittis* is "sung at every Vespers service." Simeon's canticle proclaims the child as "a 'light to enlighten the Gentiles' as well as 'the glory of [God's] people Israel.'" The Meeting between Simeon and Christ "marks the meeting of two Covenants, Old and New." [oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord](https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord)

---

**v. 33: "The Child's father and mother were amazed…"**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Notes that older authorities read "his father" instead of "and Joseph," reflecting the familiar language of the Nazareth household. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- (No further distinct commentary found on this specific verse in the pages accessed.)

---

**v. 34: "This Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel…"**

- **Ellicott:** The words start from Isaiah 8:14–15 — Christ is seen as the stone on which some fall and are bruised (Luke 20:18), while others plant their feet upon it and rise to a higher life. Primarily it speaks of two classes, but "there is nothing to exclude the thought that some may first fall, and then … rise again" (cf. Romans 11:11). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Barnes:** "Fall" denotes misery, suffering, ruin. Many expected a temporal prince and were disappointed; the proud were brought low from their self-righteousness; the nation fell into ruin. "Rising again" refers to the poor and humble who received pardon and peace and rose from sin. [biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Suggests two stages — temporary "fall of many in Israel" through unbelief during Jesus' earthly career, and subsequent "rising again" of the same persons after Pentecost. [biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Gill (Baptist/Reformed):** Emphasizes God's foreordination: Christ was "foreappointed, preordained, and set forth in God's counsel" as a stone at which some stumble and fall, and a foundation stone for others. Not the same persons — the elect rise, the reprobate fall. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Meyer (Expositor's Greek Testament):** "A forecast not necessarily beyond prophetic ken, based on insight into the career of epoch-making men." The blessing of being parent of such a child "is great, but not unmixed with sorrow." [biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm)

**On "a sign that will be spoken against":**

- **Ellicott:** An echo from Isaiah 7:14 and 8:18 — the child Immanuel was to be a sign, but not one to win acceptance. He would endure the "contradiction" of sinners (Hebrews 12:3). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Gill:** Christ is the sign of God's everlasting love; yet He is "contradicted, opposed, and treated with contempt." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm)

---

**v. 35: "…a sword will pierce your soul as well"**

- **Ellicott:** The word *rhomphaia* refers to a large barbaric Thracian sword (also in Revelation 1:16). Fulfillments: when Nazareth tried to throw Him from the hill (Luke 4:29); when Mary came in anxious fear (Matthew 12:46); when she stood by the cross (John 19:26). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-35.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-35.htm)
- **Euthymius Zigabenus (cited by Meyer):** The sword designates "the most cutting and sharp pain, which went through the heart of the Theotokos, when her Son was nailed to the cross." [biblehub.com/commentaries/meyer/luke/2-35.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/meyer/luke/2-35.htm)
- **Dean Plumptre (Pulpit Commentary):** "Dreadful alternations of faith and unbelief, of hope and fear regarding Him, which she would have to pass through." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-35.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-35.htm)
- **Orthodox (OCA):** The sword prophecy represents "the first prediction the evangelist makes concerning the Lord's coming passion." The feast's hymns declare: "And a sword shall pierce your heart, O all-pure Virgin, when you shall see your Son upon the Cross." The Theotokos presents her Son in fulfillment of the Law, but "the deeper sense … points to the Cross and to the victory to be achieved through sacrificial death." [oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord](https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord)
- **Some Restoration Movement commentators (Old & New Testament Restoration Commentary):** Note the sword can be taken two ways — Mary's suffering as mother witnessing Jesus' death, or Mary herself having to make a decision about Jesus (noting Mark 3:21 where His family thought Him insane). "Both meanings are possible." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/luke-2.html)
- **On "thoughts of many hearts revealed":** **Ellicott** connects this to the whole future career of the child — "The general result, and one of the Divine aims, will be the revelation of men's inmost thoughts." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-35.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-35.htm)

---

**v. 36–37: "There was also a prophetess named Anna…"**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Highlights Anna as a "prophetess" — one of the few women given that title in Scripture. She was of the tribe of Asher, one of the ten northern tribes, showing that not all from those tribes were lost. Her constant presence in the temple "worshiping night and day, fasting and praying" marked her as a woman of extraordinary devotion. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- (Further distinct commentary on these verses from the accessed pages was limited.)

---

**v. 38: "Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God…"**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Anna "spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem." She became one of the first evangelists, telling the faithful remnant that the Redeemer had come. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- (The Pulpit Commentary homiletics on this verse were not fully accessible for this verse in the pages fetched.)

---

**v. 39–40: Return to Nazareth; the Child grew…**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Luke emphasizes Jesus' perfect obedience to God — "when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord." Jesus was "perfectly obedient to God, even as a child." On v.40: "the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (on Marcion):** Notes that Marcion, the famous Gnostic heretic of the second century, "omitted all these passages of St. Luke's narrative in which the old Mosaic Law was spoken of with reverence." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2.htm)
- **Utley (Baptist):** On v.40, Jesus "continued to grow and become strong, increasing in wisdom; and the grace of God was upon Him" — Jesus had a normal childhood. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html)

---

**vv. 41–42: "Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover…"**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Attendance at major feasts was commanded (Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16). "It was customary for the faithful of Galilee to make these pilgrimages at feast time in large groups." At twelve, Jesus was on the brink of manhood. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **Ryle (Anglican/Evangelical):** These verses "record the only fact which we know about our Lord Jesus Christ" between infancy and the start of His public ministry. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html)

---

**vv. 43–45: Jesus remains behind; His parents search for Him**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** In large festival caravans, it was easy for parents to suppose a twelve-year-old was with relatives or friends. After a full day's journey they realized He was missing, then took another day to return to Jerusalem, and found Him on the third day of searching. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist):** Notes that Mary's anxious search — "your father and I have been seeking you anxiously (literally: in pain)" — and the three-day vigil foreshadows the three days between Jesus' death and resurrection, when "a sword will pierce through your own soul also, Mary." [desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old)

---

**vv. 46–47: Jesus found in the temple, sitting among the teachers**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** For three days, a twelve-year-old Jesus discussed God's Word and "astonished His listeners with His understanding and answers." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **Ryle:** "They found him in the temple of God — sitting in the midst of the Jewish teachers, hearing what they had to say, and asking questions about things He wished to be explained." This is an example for young persons. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html)
- **Gray's Concise Bible Commentary:** Notes three things: "(1) As a child He kept His place, asking and answering questions, but not teaching; (2) as the Son of His Divine Father He was conscious of being about His Father's business; and (3) as the child of His earthly parents He was subject unto them." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/luke-2.html)

---

**v. 48: "Child, why have You done this to us? … Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You."**

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** Highlights the contrast between Mary's "your father" (Joseph) and Jesus' response about "my Father" (God). Mary's words carry real pain — the Greek indicates they were searching "in pain." [desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Mary and Joseph were "astonished" (v.48) — not just at finding Him there, but at the scene itself and His calmness. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)

---

**v. 49: "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?"**

This verse contains a significant translation debate with theological implications.

- **Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed):** Strongly argues the correct rendering is "in my Father's house" (or literally "in my Father's"), not "about my Father's business." He notes the Greek has no word for "house" but it is implied, as we say "I'm going to my father's." The Revised Version endorses this. The natural answer to "why have you treated us so?" is about *location*: "I must be in my Father's house" — the temple. If it meant "business," it wouldn't tell them *where* to find Him. Yet Spurgeon adds that Jesus would not be idle in His Father's house: "Our Father's house is a business house." [spurgeon.org/sermons/the-first-recorded-words-of-jesus](https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-first-recorded-words-of-jesus)
- **Ryle (Anglican/Evangelical):** Defends the KJV "about my Father's business." He says the alternative "in my Father's house" "cramps and limits our Lord's words, by confining their application to one thing." "My Father's business" embraces "a far wider range of thought, and is more in keeping with the general depth and fulness of our Lord's sayings." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html)
- **Piper (Desiring God):** Notes "either translation is possible." The main point is the contrast between "your father" (Joseph) and "my Father" (God). Jesus at twelve "now recognizes his unique sonship to God, and that his mission will require of him a devotion to God's purposes so great that it takes precedence over the closest family ties." [desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** These first recorded words of Jesus are significant. "The surprise implied by these words of Jesus means that He knew that Mary and Joseph did know of His special relationship with God His Father." It must have been an item of discussion in His upbringing. In Judaism, a boy began learning his father's trade at about 12; "Jesus fulfilled this by instructing the teachers in the temple." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)
- **Utley (Baptist):** Notes this may be "Luke's attempt to refute the heresy of 'Adoptionism'" — the view that Jesus became the Son of God at His baptism, rather than being the Son from birth. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html)

---

**v. 50: "But they did not understand the statement He was making to them."**

- **Piper (Desiring God):** Luke's statement that they didn't understand is his way of telling the reader: "There's more here than meets the eye. This is the point, don't miss it." (cf. Luke 18:34). [desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old)
- (Additional distinct commentary on this verse from accessed pages was limited.)

---

**v. 51: "Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them…"**

- **Piper (Desiring God):** Jesus, though aware of His unique divine sonship, "went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them." Knowing His identity "does not make us proud or exempt us from faithful duty in small, ordinary things." [desiringgod.org/articles/jesus-obeyed-his-parents](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/jesus-obeyed-his-parents)
- **Ryle:** "He was subject unto them." The words "imply a continual habit during His residence at Nazareth, and not a single isolated act." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html)
- **Utley:** "Continued in subjection to them" is a periphrastic imperfect passive — "He was continually subject to them." The law required honoring parents. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html)
- **Guzik:** "His mother treasured up all these things in her heart." Mary's habit was not a passing emotion but a deeper meditation on God's purpose. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/)

---

**v. 52: "And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man."**

- **Ellicott:** "Here again we have nothing but a normal orderly development. With Him, as with others, wisdom widened with the years … through the same channels and by the same processes as into the souls of others — instruction, e.g., in the school of Nazareth, and attendance at its synagogue — the difference being that He, in every stage, attained the perfection of moral and spiritual wisdom which belongs to that stage; there being in Him no sin or selfishness or pride, such as checks the growth of wisdom in all others." He contrasts this with the Apocryphal Gospels where the child Jesus works miracles. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-52.htm)
- **Gill:** "As man; for neither his divine wisdom, nor the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in him, as mediator, could admit of any increase; but as he grew in body, the faculties of his soul opened, and received gradually large measures of wisdom and knowledge." The increase was in His human nature, not His divine. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-52.htm)
- **Benson (Methodist/Wesleyan):** "In the perfections of his divine nature there could be no increase; but this is spoken of his human nature … It received distinct and gradual illuminations as he advanced in years … ad modum recipientis, as that humanity was capable of receiving those manifestations." [biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/luke/2-52.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Greek word translated "increased" would be more literally "kept advancing" — a word "used for pioneers hewing down trees and brushwood which obstruct the path of an advancing army." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-52.htm)
- **Dean Plumptre (Pulpit):** "In favour with God and man" is "an addition to what had been stated in Luke 2:40, and gives the effect while that gave the cause. The Boy grew into youth, and the young Man into manhood, and the purity and lowliness and unselfish sympathy drew even then the hearts of all men." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/2-52.htm)
- **Utley:** "Jesus had a normal childhood. He is truly human (contra the Gnostics); that is how He understands us completely (cf. Hebrews 2:18; Hebrews 4:15)." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-2.html)

---

## Points of Protestant Distinctiveness (Where Traditions Differ)

**1. The "fall and rising of many" (v.34) — Predestination vs. General Outcome**

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist):** Emphasizes divine foreordination — Christ was "foreappointed, preordained" as a stone of stumbling for the reprobate and a foundation for the elect. Not the same persons. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Meyer (more modern, less Reformed):** Treats it as a natural forecast based on how "epoch-making men" always divide opinion — not necessarily a decree of individual destinies. [biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** A mediating view — the same persons may first fall through unbelief and later rise after Pentecost. [biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/luke/2-34.htm)

**2. "My Father's house" vs. "My Father's business" (v.49) — Translation Debate**

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Favors "in my Father's house" as the literal and natural reading; the answer is about *location*. [spurgeon.org/sermons/the-first-recorded-words-of-jesus](https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-first-recorded-words-of-jesus)
- **Ryle (Anglican/Evangelical):** Defends the KJV "about my Father's business" as theologically richer and "more in keeping with the general depth and fulness of our Lord's sayings." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ryl/luke-2.html)
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Says "either translation is possible" and focuses on the theological point — the contrast between "your father" and "my Father." [desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-god-at-12-years-old)

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings**

- **Orthodox (OCA):** The entire temple scene is called "The Meeting of our Lord." It "marks the meeting of two Covenants, Old and New." The Theotokos presents her Son, and the deeper sense "points to the Cross." The feast hymns declare Mary as "the pure Dove, the Ewe without blemish" who "brings the Lamb and Shepherd into the temple." Deliverance and salvation "are achieved only through the suffering and death of the crucified Lord." [oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord](https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-meeting-of-our-lord)
- On v.35, the Orthodox tradition sees the sword as specifically fulfilled at the Cross, where Mary as Theotokos suffers with her Son — a prominent theme in the Feast of the Presentation (Hypapante) liturgy.
- **Catholic perspective (Haydock, referenced on BibleHub):** On v.35, the sword piercing Mary's soul is "generally understood of the anguish which she would be called to endure as a witness of the Saviour's sufferings and death." Some ancient writers saw it also as a prediction of her martyrdom. [studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-35.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-35.html) (Catholic Bible page on BibleHub was not fully accessible in the fetches.)

**Modern Scholarship**

- **Expositor's Greek Testament (Meyer):** On v.34, treats Simeon's forecast as "not necessarily beyond prophetic ken, based on insight into the career of epoch-making men." [biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/luke/2-34.htm)
- **Ellicott:** On v.27, suggests Simeon may have been an Essene rather than a priest — "revered as possessing prophetic gifts." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-27.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-27.htm)

**Apocryphal Gospels Contrast**

- **Ellicott** on v.52 contrasts Luke's sober account of Jesus' normal development with the fantastical Apocryphal Gospels, where the child Jesus "moulds sparrows out of clay, and claps His hands and bids them fly; strikes a playmate who offends Him with dumbness, and so on ad nauseam." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-52.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/2-52.htm)
